e: Reaching an arm and the opposite leg away tends to rotate the pelvis and extend the low back. Holding neutral against that is the exercise. Reaching further is only progress if the trunk has not moved to allow it.

q: In a dead bug, what should the lower back be doing?
o: Staying in contact with the floor as the limbs extend away
Arching a little more as the arm and leg reach further out
Rotating side to side in time with the moving limbs
Lifting clear of the floor at the end of each repetition
e: The limbs pull the pelvis into anterior tilt, which lifts the lumbar spine. The abdominals resist it. Once the back lifts away the muscle being trained has already stopped working, so that moment defines the usable range.

q: In a Pallof press, what is the setup detail that makes it work?
o: Standing side-on to the cable, so its pull tries to rotate the trunk
Standing facing the cable, so its pull tries to flex the trunk forward
Standing with your back to the cable, so the press works the chest
Kneeling directly under the pulley, so the cable pulls straight down
e: The whole exercise is a rotational force being resisted. Facing towards or away from the stack removes the rotation and turns it into a press or a pull. Side-on is what creates the demand.

q: In a farmer's carry, what should the shoulders and ribcage do?
o: Shoulders set down and back, ribs down, trunk braced
Shoulders shrug up and hold, to take the strain off the neck
The trunk leans away from the load to balance it
The ribs flare up to open the chest and help breathing
e: The load pulls the shoulder girdle down and forward and tries to bend the trunk. Holding the shoulder blades set and the ribcage stacked over the pelvis is what makes it a postural exercise rather than just a grip test.

q: In a goblet squat, where should the weight sit?
o: Held close to the chest, so the trunk stays upright
Held at arm's length in front, to counterbalance the hips
Held overhead, to force the trunk to stay upright
Held at the side in one hand, to free the other arm
e: Holding the bell tight to the sternum creates a forward moment the trunk resists, which keeps the chest up and lets the hips sit down between the knees. Moving it away from the body increases the demand disproportionately and usually breaks the position.

q: In a cable triceps pushdown, what is the fault that changes the exercise?
o: Letting the upper arm swing, which brings the lats and shoulder in
Standing too close to the stack, so the cable rubs the forearms
Using a rope rather than a bar, which changes the prime mover
Extending the elbow fully at the bottom, which shifts it to the shoulder
e: Only the elbow should move. If the humerus swings, the shoulder is extending too and the lats contribute, which is a different exercise that happens to be easier. Pinning the upper arm to the ribs is the whole setup.

q: In a standing curl, what is the giveaway that the shoulder is doing the work?
o: The elbow travelling forward as the weight rises
The wrist staying straight as the weight rises
The knees staying soft throughout the set
The grip being supinated at the top of the curl
e: The biceps flexes the shoulder as well as the elbow, so when the load gets heavy the elbow drifts forward and the shoulder takes over. Keeping the elbow beside the ribs is what confines the movement to one joint.

q: In a face pull, where should the hands finish?
o: Level with or above the eyes, hands outside the elbows
At chest height, with the hands finishing inside the elbows
At the waist, with the elbows driving back past the torso
Behind the head, with the elbows pointing down
e: The point is combining horizontal abduction with external rotation. Finishing high with the hands outside the elbows produces both. Pulling to the chest with the hands low makes it an ordinary row and loses the rotation entirely.

q: In a dumbbell lateral raise, what does turning the thumb down do?
o: It turns the arm in as it rises, which many shoulders tolerate poorly
It improves the lateral deltoid's leverage, with no cost to the joint
It recruits the supraspinatus more, which protects the joint
It reduces trapezius involvement, so the deltoid works alone
e: Thumb down turns the arm in as it rises, which reduces the space under the acromion, and many shoulders tolerate it poorly. Thumb level or slightly up loads the lateral deltoid just as well.

q: In an assisted pull-up, what is the most common setup error?
o: Selecting so much assistance that the muscles barely work
Kneeling on the pad rather than standing on it for the set
Using the neutral handles rather than the wide pronated ones
Holding the top position rather than lowering straight away
e: The weight stack is counterweight: more plates means an easier rep. It is the one machine where a heavier selection makes the exercise lighter, which is the mistake almost everyone makes on their first attempt.

q: Machines only, and the target is the rhomboids and middle trapezius. Which machine and which setting?
o: A seated row, pulling with the elbows high and wide
A seated row, pulling with the elbows tucked low
A lat pulldown with a wide grip, pulled to the chest
A chest press machine, retracting at the start
e: Elbows high and wide makes the movement horizontal abduction with scapular retraction, which is what the mid-back muscles do. Tucking the elbows on the same machine biases the lats instead, so the setting matters more than the machine.

q: Machines only, and the aim is pectoralis major with the elbow excluded. Which one?
o: A chest fly machine with the elbows fixed on pads
A chest press machine with a narrow neutral grip
An assisted dip machine, leaning forward for the chest
A cable pushdown with the elbows flared out
e: Fixing the elbow angle leaves the shoulder as the only moving joint, so the triceps cannot contribute. Any pressing machine involves elbow extension by design, which is the difference between a press and a fly.

q: Which machine trains the hip flexors, and why is it uncommon?
o: A cable with an ankle strap; few gyms have a hip flexor machine
The leg extension; it flexes the hip as the leg lifts the pad
The leg press with high feet; the hip flexes deeply at the bottom
The hip adduction machine; the hip flexors squeeze the pads in
e: Resisted hip flexion needs a cable and a strap in most gyms. The leg extension moves the knee, not the hip, and neither of the others flexes it. The hip flexors are among the least catered-for muscle groups on a standard gym floor.

q: Which machine would you use for the erector spinae working dynamically?
o: A back extension bench, letting the spine flex and extend through range
A seated row without the chest pad, holding the back upright throughout
A leg press, pressing the lower back into the pad
An abdominal crunch machine, working the trunk through range
e: Moving the spine into extension against gravity is what loads the erectors concentrically. A chest-supported row deliberately removes them, and the crunch machine trains the opposite action.

q: Only a cable stack is available and the target is the gluteus maximus. What setup?
o: A cable kickback or pull-through, both resisting hip extension
A cable curl from a low pulley, keeping the hips still
A cable lateral raise, standing on one leg so the hip works as well
A cable rotation from the side, turning through the hips as you pull
e: Glute max extends the hip, so the resistance has to oppose hip extension. A pull-through gives a hinge pattern against the stack; a kickback isolates it. Neither is as loadable as a hip thrust, but both work with one machine.

q: A client needs the lats but cannot grip a bar because of a hand injury. What machine option remains?
o: A pullover machine or a pulldown with wrist cuffs, which need no grip
A seated row with a thick handle, which spreads the load in the hand
An assisted pull-up, where the counterweight reduces the grip needed
A cable curl with a strap, which takes the load off the fingers
e: Both remaining options transmit force through the elbow or upper arm rather than the hand. Any rowing or pulling movement held by the fingers is out, which is a common constraint and one machines happen to solve well.

q: Which machine loads the hamstrings eccentrically with the least skill required?
o: A seated or lying leg curl, lowering the weight slowly
A leg extension, lowering the weight slowly each rep
A leg press, lowering the sled slowly towards the chest
The hip adduction machine, opening the legs slowly
e: The leg curl's fixed path means the only variable is tempo, so lengthening under load is just a matter of lowering slowly. A Nordic curl trains the same thing far harder but needs technique and a tolerance most beginners do not have.

q: A client feels a lat pulldown entirely in their arms. What do you change first?
o: Cue the elbows to drive down and back, before changing the machine
Increase the weight, so the arms can no longer do the work alone
Widen the grip as far as the bar allows, so the arms are taken out
Raise the thigh pad, so the body can lean back into the pull
e: The lats move the upper arm, so cue the elbow: 'elbow towards your back pocket' names the lat's two ends. Thinking about the hands recruits the elbow flexors. Try the cue before touching the settings.

q: Which machine most closely reproduces the demand of a farmer's carry?
o: None of them; no fixed machine reproduces walking under load
The shrug machine, which loads the traps in the same hanging position
The seated row, which holds the shoulder blades back under load
The cable stack with heavy handles, held at the sides for time
e: A shrug loads the traps and a row loads the back, but neither asks the trunk to stay stacked while moving under an external load. Some qualities are only trainable away from machines, and this is one of the clearest examples.

q: Which machine would you select to train knee extension for a client who cannot bear weight through the leg?
o: The leg extension, since the body is seated and the leg hangs free
The leg press, since the back is supported and the sled is guided
The hack squat, since the shoulders are supported on pads
The Smith machine squat, since the bar path is fixed
e: Bearing weight is exactly what the other three require. A leg extension loads the knee with the body supported, which is why it appears so often in early rehabilitation despite being an unfashionable exercise.

q: Which two machines together cover both functions of the hamstrings?
o: A leg curl for the knee and a back extension for the hip
A leg curl and a leg extension, which between them cover the knee
A leg press with high feet and a hip adduction machine for magnus
A hack squat for the hip and a calf machine for the knee end
e: The hamstrings flex the knee and extend the hip. A curl covers the first and a hip extension movement covers the second. Training only one leaves half the group's function untouched, which is the argument against relying on the curl alone.

q: Rowing machine: what is the correct sequence of the drive?
o: Legs, then hips and back, then arms
Arms, then back, then legs
Legs and arms together, then the back
Back, then legs, then arms
e: The strongest segment goes first and the weakest last. Legs drive the seat back, the hips and trunk swing open, and only then do the arms finish the pull. Reversing it means the arms try to move a load the legs should have shifted.

q: Rowing machine: roughly how is the work distributed?
o: Most from the legs, then the hips and back, least from the arms
Most from the arms, then the hips and back, least from the legs
Evenly split across the legs, the back and the arms
Most from the back, then the arms, least from the legs
e: The legs drive the seat back first, the trunk swings open, and the arms only finish the pull, so the legs supply most of the power. A split of about 60% legs is often quoted; the exact figures vary between coaching sources.

q: Rowing machine: what is the most common fault on the recovery?
o: Bending the knees before the handle has passed them
Straightening the arms too early, before the body swings forward
Pausing briefly at the catch before starting the next drive
Sliding forward too slowly, so the recovery takes longer than the drive
e: The recovery reverses the drive: arms away, then hinge forward, then bend the knees. Breaking the knees early puts them in the handle's path, which forces an awkward lift over the top and wastes the stroke.

q: Stationary bike: how should the saddle height be set?
o: So the knee keeps a slight bend at the bottom of the stroke
So the leg straightens fully, with the heel on the pedal at the bottom
So the knee stays at about ninety degrees at the bottom
So both feet can rest flat on the floor while seated
e: Too low and the knee never opens, which loads the front of the joint and limits power. Too high and the hips rock side to side reaching for the pedal. A small residual bend at the bottom is the target, and it is the single most commonly wrong setting in any gym.

q: Stationary bike: what does a saddle set too high produce?
o: Rocking hips and strain at the back of the knee
Pain at the front of the knee from deep flexion
An inability to reach the handlebars comfortably
Excessive quadriceps fatigue and nothing else
e: Reaching for the bottom of the stroke makes the pelvis tip side to side and overextends the knee, which stresses the hamstring attachment behind it. A saddle too low does the opposite and irritates the front of the knee.

q: Treadmill: what does raising the incline do to the muscular demand?
o: Increases the demand on the hip extensors, the glutes and hamstrings
Increases the demand on the anterior tibialis more than anything else
Reduces the demand on the calf complex as the ankle angle changes
Shifts the work to the quadriceps only, as the knees bend more
e: Climbing requires more hip extension to drive the body upward, so the glutes and hamstrings do more. It is also a way of raising intensity without raising speed, which matters for anyone whose joints do not tolerate faster running.

q: Treadmill: what is wrong with holding the handrails?
o: It offloads bodyweight, so the work is less than the display suggests
It improves posture, but at the cost of reducing the balance training
It has no real effect beyond making the walk more comfortable
It increases the cardiovascular demand by adding the arms to the work
e: Leaning on the rails transfers part of the body's weight into the arms, so both the muscular and the metabolic cost fall. The machine has no way of knowing, so the calorie and workload readouts become fiction.

q: Stair climber: which muscle group does it emphasise compared with a flat treadmill walk?
o: The hip extensors, especially gluteus maximus
The anterior tibialis, lifting the toes each step
The adductors, holding the knees in line
The latissimus dorsi, if the rails are held
e: Stepping up is repeated hip and knee extension against bodyweight, which is why it is felt in the glutes. Flat walking has far less hip extension range and demand per step.

q: Elliptical: what is its defining characteristic?
o: A fixed, low-impact path, which also reduces the balance demand
A free path that trains coordination and balance with each stride
Greater muscular demand than running at the same heart rate
A mainly upper-body stimulus, since the arms drive the handles
e: The feet never leave the pedals, so impact is low and the stride is dictated by the machine. That makes it useful when impact must be limited, and less useful when the aim is running-specific carry-over.

q: Assault or air bike: what distinguishes it from a standard stationary bike?
o: The arms drive as well as the legs, so more muscle mass is working
It uses magnetic rather than air resistance, so it is quieter to ride
It cannot be ridden seated, so the legs work standing throughout
It loads the arms only, while the legs simply follow the pedals
e: Moving handles mean the upper body contributes, which raises the metabolic cost sharply for the same leg effort. The fan also means resistance rises with effort, so it self-scales rather than needing a level selected.

q: Ski erg: which muscles does the pulling action emphasise?
o: The latissimus dorsi and triceps, with the trunk flexing to assist
The biceps and anterior deltoid, with the legs extending to assist
The quadriceps, with the arms only guiding the handles down
The rotator cuff, holding the shoulders stable as the arms lower
e: Pulling from overhead down past the hips is shoulder extension plus elbow extension, which is lats and triceps. The trunk contributes by flexing, which is why it is felt in the abdominals as much as the arms.

q: A client wants a cardio machine that loads the hip extensors and tolerates a sore knee. What fits best?
o: An inclined treadmill walk
A stair climber
A rowing machine at high resistance
A leg press performed quickly
e: Incline walking increases hip extension demand without the repeated deep knee flexion of stair climbing or the compressive load of rowing hard. The last option is not a cardio machine at all.

q: What happens to a resistance band's tension through the range?
o: It rises as the band stretches, so the exercise is hardest at the end
It stays constant throughout the range, just like the tension in a cable
It falls as the band stretches, so the start is the hardest part
It peaks in the middle of the range, then falls towards the end
e: Elastic resistance is a function of how far it has been stretched. That makes bands useful where the muscle is strongest at the short end, and a poor match where the hardest part of the lift is at the start.

q: What is the defining property of cable resistance compared with a free weight?
o: The pull can be set in any direction, with fairly constant tension
Its tension increases through the range, in the same way as a band's
It needs more stabiliser work than a dumbbell of the same load
It can only pull vertically, in the same line as a free weight
e: A free weight always pulls straight down, so the difficulty depends on the limb's angle to gravity. A cable pulls towards the pulley wherever that is, which is why it can load positions gravity cannot reach.

q: Why is a dumbbell lateral raise hardest when the arm is horizontal?
o: The moment arm between the shoulder and the weight is longest there
The deltoid is at its weakest length at that point in the range
The supraspinatus switches off at that point, leaving the deltoid alone
Gravity acts more strongly on the weight at that height
e: The load always falls straight down, so the torque at the shoulder depends on how far the weight is horizontally from the joint. At shoulder height that distance is at its maximum, which is why the last part of the raise feels disproportionately hard.

q: Why is a barbell curl hardest at about ninety degrees of elbow flexion?
o: The forearm is horizontal, so the moment arm at the elbow is longest
The biceps is fully shortened there, so it has little left to give
The brachialis stops working at that angle, leaving the biceps alone
The wrist flexors take over past that point and tire first
e: Same principle as the lateral raise. Torque is the weight multiplied by its horizontal distance from the joint, and that distance peaks when the moving segment is parallel to the floor. Nothing about the muscle changes; the leverage does.

q: Where is a squat hardest, and why?
o: Near the bottom, where the moment arms at hip and knee are longest
At the top, where the bar is highest and the legs are nearly straight
In the middle, where the bar is moving at its fastest
Where the knees pass the toes, which loads the knee joint most
e: Depth increases the horizontal distance from the bar to both the hip and the knee, which is what makes the torque demand peak there. It is also why partial squats allow so much more weight without training the hard part.

q: How does a well-designed machine cam try to improve on a free weight?
o: By varying the resistance through the range to match the strength curve
By removing the eccentric phase, so there is less soreness afterwards
By increasing the resistance continuously through the range, like a band
By eliminating the need to stabilise, so the prime movers work harder
e: A free weight is hardest where the leverage is worst, not where the muscle is strongest. A cam alters the effective load through the range to fit the muscle better. Whether any given machine succeeds is a separate question.

q: What does a dumbbell bench press offer over a barbell version?
o: More range and more stabiliser demand, at the cost of absolute load
More absolute load for the same effort, since each arm works on its own
Less shoulder involvement, since the hands can turn inward
A fixed path that is easier to learn than the barbell's
e: The hands are free, so they can travel lower than a bar would allow and must be controlled independently. That is more range and more demand on the small stabilising muscles, and it is why the same person presses less with dumbbells.

q: Why can a kettlebell be swung in ways a dumbbell cannot?
o: Its mass hangs below the handle, which suits swings and other ballistics
It is always heavier than a dumbbell, so the hips have to drive it
Its centre of mass sits right at the handle, which keeps the swing close in
It cannot be lifted slowly, so it has to be swung to be useful
e: The offset centre of mass creates an arc and a pendulum effect, which is what makes swings, cleans and snatches work. A dumbbell's mass sits in line with the hand, which suits controlled lifting rather than ballistics.

q: What does adding chains or bands to a barbell achieve?
o: The load rises as the lift moves into its stronger range
A reduction in the load at the top of the lift, where the bar slows
A constant load throughout, with less bar whip on heavy sets
An increase in stabiliser demand only, with the load unchanged
e: Most lifts are weakest at the bottom and strongest near lockout, so a constant barbell load underloads the top. Chains lift off the floor and bands stretch as the bar rises, adding resistance where there is capacity for it; this is accommodating resistance.

q: A client cannot load a movement heavily but needs a challenge at the end range. What implement suits?
o: A band, which is hardest where it is most stretched
A dumbbell, which is hardest at the end of the range
A kettlebell, whose offset mass loads the end range
A weight stack machine with a cam that flattens the curve
e: The band's ascending profile puts the hardest part where the muscle is short, which is exactly the end range. It is why bands suit things like glute bridges and external rotation work where the top is otherwise trivially easy.

q: Why does a cable lateral raise feel different from a dumbbell one?
o: The cable keeps tension at the bottom, where a dumbbell has none
The cable is heavier at the top, where the dumbbell gets easier
The cable takes the supraspinatus out, leaving the deltoid alone
The cable changes the prime mover from the lateral deltoid to the upper traps
e: With the arm hanging, a dumbbell produces almost no torque at the shoulder because it sits directly under the joint. A cable pulling from the side keeps loading it there, which is why the bottom of the range suddenly has something to do.

q: Sumo against conventional deadlift: what changes?
o: Sumo is more upright, with a shorter bar path and more adductor and quad work
Sumo increases spinal loading and range, since the torso leans further forward
Conventional removes the hamstrings, since the hips start lower
They are mechanically identical, differing only in where the hands go
e: The wide stance lowers the hips, shortens the distance the bar travels and turns the femurs out, which brings the adductors in and reduces the forward lean. Neither is easier in general; they suit different proportions.

q: High-bar against low-bar back squat: what changes?
o: Low bar allows more forward lean and hip work; high bar is more upright and knee-heavy
High bar allows more forward lean and hip work; low bar is more upright and knee-heavy
Low bar removes the quadriceps; high bar removes the hip extensors entirely
Bar position changes only comfort; the joint angles stay the same
e: Where the bar sits determines the torso angle needed to keep it over the midfoot. Further down the back means more lean and a longer moment arm at the hip. Same exercise name, meaningfully different distribution.

q: Leg press against hack squat: what is the practical difference?
o: The hack squat moves the body like a squat; the leg press fixes it
The leg press loads the hamstrings, and the hack squat does not load them
They load entirely different muscles, despite the similar foot position
The hack squat removes the quadriceps by keeping the torso upright
e: Both extend the knee and hip against a fixed path. The difference is orientation and how much of the body moves, which affects comfort and spinal loading more than it affects which muscles work.

q: Pull-up against lat pulldown: what is the substantive difference?
o: The pull-up moves the body, and bodyweight is its lightest load
The pulldown trains different muscles, since the body stays seated
The pull-up removes the biceps, since the body moves towards the bar
The pulldown allows no scapular movement, since the thigh pad fixes it
e: The muscle actions are the same. What differs is what moves and how the load is set: the pulldown lets you select anything from very light upward, while the pull-up starts at your bodyweight and needs a machine or a band to go lower.

q: Seated row against bent-over barbell row: what does the seated version remove?
o: The demand on the erectors and hips to hold a hinge under load
The latissimus dorsi, which the seat takes out of the pull
The biceps, since the handle sets the elbow at a fixed angle
The scapular retractors, since the pad blocks the shoulder blades
e: The pulling is much the same. Sitting with the chest supported removes the isometric back and hip work that makes the bent-over version fatiguing well beyond the muscles being trained.

q: Front squat against back squat: which is more limited by upper-back strength?
o: The front squat, since the load in front tries to fold the trunk forward
The back squat, since the bar sits right on the traps and loads them directly
Neither; both are limited by leg strength before the upper back
Both equally, since the bar weight is the same in each
e: A front-racked bar constantly tries to pull the torso forward, so the thoracic extensors and the rack position often fail before the legs do. It is why many people front squat considerably less than they back squat.

q: Goblet squat against back squat for a beginner: what is the argument for the goblet?
o: The load in front keeps the trunk upright, so position corrects itself
It loads the legs more heavily than a bar on the back can
It removes the need for ankle mobility at the very bottom of the squat
It trains different muscles, which suit a beginner better
e: Holding the weight at the chest makes the torso stay upright, so the position largely corrects itself. That is the reason to use it: not that it is lighter, but that the position is harder to get wrong.

q: A client cannot perform a full press-up. What is the first regression to try?
o: Raise the hands onto a bench or box, so less bodyweight is carried
Drop to the knees straight away, so the lever is shorter and lighter
Cut the range to the top few centimetres of the press-up
Move to a machine chest press until the strength is there
e: Elevating the hands keeps the whole body in one line and simply tilts it, which reduces load while preserving the pattern and the trunk demand. Going to the knees also works but removes the hip and trunk position that makes a press-up worth doing.

q: How would you make a press-up harder without adding external weight?
o: Raise the feet, so more bodyweight sits over the hands
Widen the hands as far as possible, to lengthen the lever
Increase the repetitions only, keeping the position the same
Hold the top position for longer, with the arms locked
e: Tilting the body the other way shifts more mass towards the shoulders. It is the same adjustment as the regression, run in reverse, which is why hand and foot height is the main dial on any press-up variation.

q: A client cannot do a single pull-up. Which progression preserves the movement best?
o: Band-assisted pull-ups or slow lowering from the top
Lat pulldowns only, until the pulldown weight exceeds bodyweight
Biceps curls to build the arm strength that pull-ups need
Isometric holds at the bottom from a dead hang
e: Both options keep the actual movement and reduce the load or use only the strong phase. A pulldown is a reasonable supplement but never requires moving bodyweight, which is the specific capacity being built.

q: What is the standard regression when a client cannot squat to depth without rounding?
o: Squat to a box set at a height they can control
Add weight to the bar to force a better position
Squat on an unstable surface to wake up the core
Increase the reps at partial depth only
e: A box gives an unambiguous target and stops the descent at the depth the client can control. It also lets depth be lowered a little at a time, which turns depth into a progression rather than a pass or fail.

q: What makes a deadlift easier without reducing the weight on the bar?
o: Starting higher, as in a rack pull
Starting from a deficit, standing on a low plate
Using a wider, snatch-width grip on the bar
Holding the lockout at the top for longer
e: Raising the start shortens the range and skips the hardest part off the floor, where the leverages are worst. Standing on a plate does the reverse, which is why a deficit is the harder variant rather than the easier one.

q: A client cannot hold a plank with a neutral spine for more than a few seconds. What do you change first?
o: Raise the hands onto a bench to shorten the lever
Add a light plate to the back so the trunk has to brace harder
Extend the hold time and accept some sagging
Move to a side plank, which is easier to hold
e: Shortening the lever reduces the demand while the position is still being held correctly. Accepting a poor position trains the compensation rather than the muscle, and time is only a useful variable once the position holds.

q: Of a static split squat, a walking lunge and a Bulgarian split squat, which is the easiest place to start single-leg work?
o: Static split squat: both feet stay planted between reps
Walking lunge: the momentum of each step helps carry you through
Bulgarian split squat: the bench supports the rear leg throughout
All three are equally demanding, since each is one leg at a time
e: The static split squat has the most stable base, with both feet fixed. Walking adds a transition and balance demand on every step, and elevating the rear foot shifts more load to the front leg.

q: What is the correct progression of surfaces for balance work?
o: Stable to less stable: floor, then foam pad, then wobble board
Least stable first, so that the floor feels easy by comparison later
Foam pad, then floor, then wobble board, to vary the stimulus
Any order, since each surface is equally unstable
e: Surface is one of the dials: floor, then softer or moving surfaces. Turn one dial at a time, and keep unstable surfaces away from heavy loads, since base stability and load move in opposite directions.

q: According to the progression hierarchy, what should be the last variable you change?
o: The load
The tempo
The rest between sets
The exercise selection
e: The kettlebell course's order is pace within the set, then longer sets, then less rest, then fewer side switches, then a harder grip, and load last. Adding weight first uses up the easiest option and hides the others.

q: A client can hold a single-leg stance but wobbles. What is the next step rather than making it harder?
o: Hold it longer, or add a reach while the foot stays planted
Move straight to a BOSU ball, so the ankle has to work harder
Add a dumbbell to the hand to load the stance leg
Close the eyes to take away visual feedback
e: Consolidate before destabilising. Adding time or a controlled limb movement raises the demand within a position that is nearly mastered, where an unstable surface or removing vision usually collapses the pattern entirely.

q: How do you regress a Nordic curl?
o: Assist with a band, or limit the range to what can be controlled
Perform it faster, so that less time is spent in the hardest range
Add weight to the upper body to slow the descent
Switch to a leg extension, which trains the same muscle
e: The exercise is defined by controlled lengthening, so the two useful dials are how much help is given and how far down the control extends. Speeding it up removes the eccentric quality that is the whole point.

q: How would you progress a glute bridge?
o: Feet raised, then a single leg, then load across the hips
Keep adding repetitions until each set passes fifty
Add an unstable surface under the shoulders, then the feet
Hold at the bottom rather than the top, then add load
e: Range, then limb number, then load. Each step raises the demand on the same pattern in a defined order, which is what a progression is, as distinct from simply doing more of the easy version.

q: Seated to standing to single-arm overhead press: what is being progressed?
o: The stability demand on the trunk and hips
The load on the deltoid, which rises with each step in the sequence
The range of motion at the shoulder, which grows at each step
The elbow extension demand, as the triceps take more of the press
e: The pressing muscles do the same job throughout. What changes is how much the trunk and hips must resist, first the load tipping you back, then the load twisting you sideways. Weight usually has to fall at each step.

q: A client finds a Romanian deadlift uncomfortable in the lower back. What is the most useful first change?
o: Shorten the range to where the spine stays still, and check the hips lead
Add weight so the trunk has to brace harder against the bar
Round the back on purpose, so the hamstrings are under less tension at the bottom
Switch to a full deadlift from the floor to share the load
e: The exercise is defined by the spine staying still while the hips move. If the back is complaining, either the range has exceeded hamstring length or the spine is moving. Shortening the range fixes the first and exposes the second.

q: What makes a carry harder on the trunk and shoulders without changing the weight?
o: Carrying it on one side, or overhead instead of at the side
Walking faster, with a longer stride, over the same distance
Walking further at the same pace before setting it down
Using a thicker handle, so the grip has to work harder
e: Position changes the demand more than distance does. One-sided loading adds an anti-lateral-flexion requirement, and overhead adds a shoulder stability requirement. Distance and speed change the conditioning element rather than the stability one.

q: A client can leg press comfortably but cannot squat. What does that tell you?
o: The limit is probably balance, trunk control or mobility, not leg strength
Their quadriceps are too weak to control the deeper range a free squat needs
The leg press is the harder exercise, so the squat should follow
They need a heavier squat load, so the pattern has to settle
e: The leg press supports the back, fixes the path and removes balance. If the legs can press a substantial load, the missing pieces are the things the machine was providing. That is where to look rather than at leg strength.

q: The lat pulldown is occupied. What is the closest substitute?
o: A band pulldown anchored overhead, or an assisted pull-up
A seated cable row with a wide grip, pulled to the lower chest
A biceps curl on the cable stack
A face pull with the rope at eye height
e: The defining feature is resistance from overhead producing shoulder adduction. A band or an assisted pull-up keeps that line of pull; a row changes it to horizontal, which trains an overlapping but different emphasis.

q: No leg curl machine. How do you train the hamstrings at their knee end?
o: A Nordic curl, a sliding leg curl or a band leg curl
A Romanian deadlift with dumbbells, keeping a soft knee
A 45 degree back extension
A leg press with the feet high
e: Knee flexion against resistance is the requirement. All three substitutes provide it. The other options are all hip extension, which trains the same muscles through their other action and is not a replacement.

q: No bench available. What replaces a barbell bench press?
o: A floor press or a press-up variation
A standing overhead press with the barbell
A lat pulldown to the chest
A standing barbell upright row
e: A floor press keeps the horizontal pressing pattern with a shortened range, and press-ups keep it with bodyweight. An overhead press is a vertical push, and the other two are not presses at all.

q: No barbell for hip thrusts. What are the options?
o: A single-leg bridge, a banded bridge, or a dumbbell across the hips
A leg extension with the seat reclined as far as it goes
A seated calf raise with the load on the knees
A back squat with the bar held low, which also peaks the glutes at lockout
e: The requirement is resistance to hip extension with peak load near lockout. Removing a leg, adding a band or holding weight on the hips all achieve it. A squat loads the same muscle but peaks at the opposite end of the range.

q: No calf machine. What is the substitute?
o: A single-leg calf raise off a step, holding a dumbbell if needed
A leg press with the feet high on the platform, pushing through the heels
A seated leg curl with the toes pointed
A wall sit held up on the toes
e: Removing a leg doubles the relative load and a step restores the full range. Knee position still selects between gastrocnemius and soleus, so bend the knee if soleus is the target.

q: No cable machine. What replaces cable work most faithfully?
o: Resistance bands, since both can pull from any direction
Dumbbells, since both let each arm work on its own
A barbell, since both allow a smooth, fixed line
Fixed-path machines, since both are loaded from a pin-selected weight stack
e: Direction is the property that matters. Only a band can be anchored anywhere and pull from that angle. The trade-off is that tension rises through the range where a cable's stays roughly constant.

q: No leg extension machine, and the client needs knee extension work without loading the spine. What works?
o: A Spanish squat with a band behind the knees, or a reverse Nordic
A back squat kept high, above parallel, so the knees do most work
A walking lunge with a short stride
A stiff-legged deadlift with light dumbbells
e: Both substitutes load knee extension with the trunk near vertical and no external load on the shoulders. A reverse Nordic also lengthens rectus femoris at the hip, which the machine cannot do at all.

q: Travelling with no equipment and the goal is hip extension strength. What is the best available option?
o: Single-leg glute bridges and single-leg hinges
Bodyweight squats in high-rep sets, to fifty or more
Press-ups with the feet raised on a chair
Plank holds, building up to several minutes
e: Removing a leg is the only way to raise relative load without equipment. Both options keep the emphasis on hip extension, where a bodyweight squat shares the work with the knee and is usually too easy to be a stimulus.

q: No rowing machine. What trains the same movement pattern?
o: A hinge plus a horizontal pull, such as an RDL alternated with a row
A lat pulldown, which covers the pull and uses the same muscles
A leg press, since the legs supply most of the power in the rowing stroke
A biceps curl, since the arms finish every rowing stroke
e: The stroke is a leg drive, a hip extension and a pull. No single substitute reproduces the sequence, so the honest answer is to train the components. The conditioning element needs a separate machine.

q: A client has only a set of light dumbbells and needs a genuine lower-body stimulus. What is the strategy?
o: Single-leg variations, so the light load becomes a meaningful relative load
Repetitions into the hundreds, so the light load finally becomes a stimulus
A switch to upper-body work, since the legs are beyond the dumbbells
Jumping added to every exercise, so speed makes up for the light load
e: Halving the base of support roughly doubles the load per leg before anything is held. That turns light dumbbells into an adequate stimulus for split squats, single-leg RDLs and step-ups, which repetitions alone will not do.

q: Where should a spotter stand and place their hands for a barbell bench press?
o: Behind the head of the bench, hands close to the bar but not touching it
At the side of the bench, with the hands cupped under the lifter's elbows
Behind the head, with the hands wrapped firmly round the lifter's wrists
Standing over the lifter, with the hands on the bar throughout
e: The bar is what needs catching, so the spotter is positioned to take it and stays close without adding or subtracting force. Spotting the wrists or elbows gives no control of the bar, and holding it throughout means neither party knows what the lifter lifted.

q: What is the correct way to bail out of a heavy dumbbell bench press alone?
o: Lower them out to the sides and set them down, keeping control
Let them fall behind the head, well clear of the chest and face
Drop them straight down onto the chest, then roll them off
Roll them down the torso to the thighs, then sit up
e: Sideways is the one direction that is clear of the body and the floor space of others. Behind the head risks the shoulders and anyone walking past, and letting them fall inward is exactly what a spotter exists to prevent.

q: How should the safety pins in a squat rack be set?
o: Just below the lowest point the bar reaches in the rep
At the height of the lifter's shoulders when standing
At the very bottom of the rack, as low as they go
Not at all, if a spotter is standing behind the lifter
e: The pins have to catch the bar in the failure position, which means just below the bottom of the movement. Set too high and they block the rep, set too low and the lifter is pinned before they engage.

q: How do you spot a barbell back squat?
o: Close behind, ready to assist round the chest or under the arms
Holding the bar lightly with both hands throughout the whole set
At one side, ready to lift one end of the bar if needed
Behind, with the hands on the lifter's hips to steady them
e: The lifter and the bar move as one unit, so the spot supports the whole torso. A one-sided spot on the bar would tip it, and holding the hips does not stop the bar descending.

q: What is the reason for using collars on a loaded barbell?
o: They stop plates sliding off if the bar tilts, unbalancing it
They add measurably to the total weight, which then has to be counted
They stop the bar spinning in the hands during the lift
They are only needed in competition, where plates must be secured
e: An uneven bar is the danger, not a plate hitting the floor. If one side slides while the other does not, the bar becomes suddenly asymmetric under load, which is how people get injured on lifts they can otherwise handle.

q: What is the safest way to fail a deadlift?
o: Keep hold and lower it under control to the floor
Release the bar at the top and step back out of the way
Drop it from mid-shin height once the bar starts to slow
Twist to one side while lowering, so the bar clears the knees
e: A deadlift is the one big lift where failure has a safe default, because the bar can simply go back where it came from. Dropping it risks feet and bar; twisting under load is how backs get hurt.

q: What should a spotter establish before the set begins?
o: The number of reps, whether a lift-off is wanted, and the signal for help
The lifter's one-rep maximum, so the spotter knows how close to failure they are
Whether the lifter prefers a wide or close grip on the bar
The rest interval to be used between this set and the next
e: A spot only works if both people expect the same thing. Ambiguity about when to intervene is what produces either a ruined set or a missed catch. The conversation costs ten seconds.

q: Why should a treadmill's safety clip be attached?
o: It stops the belt if the user falls or moves too far back
It measures heart rate through contact with the clothing at the waist
It records the workout data to the user's account
It stops the incline changing while the belt is moving
e: The clip is a dead man's switch. Without it, a fall means the belt keeps running under the person on it, which is the mechanism behind most treadmill injuries.

q: What is the risk when returning a heavy cable or weight stack at the end of a set?
o: Letting it drop uncontrolled, jolting the joint and damaging the machine
Returning it too slowly, which adds unplanned time under tension to the set
Standing too close to the stack as the plates come to rest
Using both hands, which lets the stronger side take over
e: The last eccentric is still a loaded eccentric, and releasing suddenly puts a jerk through the joint at its end range. Controlling the return to the stack is part of the set, not an afterthought.

q: A client is pressing overhead and the bar starts drifting forward. What is the appropriate action?
o: Have them lower it under control to the shoulders; the rep has failed
Push the elbows from behind to help them finish the rep
Have them lean back further, so the bar comes back over the shoulders
Have them let go of the bar and step back out of the way
e: Once the bar is forward of the shoulder it cannot be pressed up, and leaning back to compensate loads the lumbar spine instead. Bringing it down to the front rack is the controlled way out. Overhead lifts are poorly suited to spotting at all.

q: What usually determines the hardest point of a free-weight exercise?
o: Where the moment arm from the joint to the load is longest
Where the muscle is fully shortened and has the least force left
Where the bar is moving fastest, so momentum is hardest to control
Where the joint reaches its end range and the tissues are most stretched
e: Torque is the load multiplied by its horizontal distance from the joint. That distance peaks when the limb or the bar is furthest out sideways, which is almost always where the lift stalls. The muscle's own strength curve matters less than the geometry.

q: Where is a bench press hardest, and why?
o: Near the chest, where the bar is furthest horizontally from the shoulder
At lockout, where the triceps are at their shortest and have least force
In the middle, where the bar is moving at its fastest
As the bar leaves the rack, before the arms have set
e: At the bottom the upper arm is furthest from the shoulder joint horizontally, so the torque demand peaks. Lockout is easy because the bar sits almost directly over the joint. It is why a board press or a pin press allows so much more weight.

q: Where is a dip hardest?
o: At the bottom, where the shoulder is most extended and the elbow most bent
At lockout, where the triceps are at their shortest and the elbows straight
At the midpoint, where the elbows pass ninety degrees
Nowhere in particular; the demand is constant throughout
e: Depth increases the distance from the hands to both the shoulder and the elbow, so both joints face their largest demand at once. That is also the position most likely to trouble a shoulder, which is why depth is worth choosing deliberately.

q: Where is an overhead press hardest for most people?
o: Just above the shoulders, before the bar passes the head
At full lockout overhead, as the triceps finish the press
At the moment of unracking the bar from the stands
Once the bar is past the head, as the arms straighten
e: Starting from the shoulders, the bar is at its furthest horizontal distance from the shoulder joint and the deltoid has poor leverage. Once it is past the head the load sits almost above the joint, and the position becomes a matter of stability rather than force.

q: With a dumbbell held between the feet, where is a lying leg curl hardest?
o: At the start, with the shin horizontal and the moment arm longest
At full knee flexion, where the hamstrings are shortest
In the middle of the range, with the knee bent to about forty-five degrees
At the point the hips start to lift off the pad
e: With the leg straight the dumbbell sits furthest horizontally from the knee. As the knee bends the shin rotates upward and the moment arm shortens, so the lift gets easier as the hamstrings shorten; machines with a cam reshape that curve.

q: On a plate-loaded seated leg extension, where is the lift hardest?
o: At full extension, with the shin horizontal
At the start, with the knee fully bent
In the middle of the range, at about forty-five degrees
At the point the hips leave the seat
e: The moment arm at the knee is longest when the shin is parallel to the floor, which is the finish. That is also where the quadriceps are shortest, which is why the last few degrees are where people fail and why the top of the range gets cut.

q: Where is a Romanian deadlift hardest?
o: At the bottom, where the bar is furthest horizontally from the hip
At lockout, where the glutes are fully shortened and squeezing hard
At the midpoint, as the bar passes the knees
Where the knees begin to bend on the way down
e: Hinging forward increases the horizontal distance from the bar to the hip joint, which is what makes the bottom the demanding part. It also coincides with the hamstrings being at their longest, which is why range should be set by position rather than ambition.

q: Where is a hip thrust hardest?
o: At the top, with the hip extended and the bar highest
At the bottom, with the hips close to the floor and fully flexed
In the middle, as the hips pass bench height
Nowhere in particular; it is constant throughout
e: At lockout the torso is horizontal, so the hip sits furthest horizontally from the shoulders on the bench and the hip extensors' demand peaks. That is the opposite of a squat, which is why both are worth doing.

q: Why does restricting an exercise to a partial range allow so much more weight?
o: The part kept usually skips the position where the moment arm is longest
Muscles are simply stronger when they contract through a shorter distance
Shorter ranges recruit more motor units in the working muscle
The nervous system adapts faster to a range it uses more often
e: Partial ranges skip the hard part by definition. That is legitimate when the aim is to overload a specific portion or to work around an injury, and misleading when it is treated as the same lift with a bigger number on it.

q: What is a sticking point, stated mechanically?
o: The angle where demand outstrips force, usually where the moment arm peaks
The point where the muscle runs out of glycogen partway through the rep
The moment the nervous system inhibits the movement to protect the joint
The top of the range, where the muscle is shortest and weakest
e: It is where torque required crosses torque available. Since required torque peaks with the moment arm, the sticking point is usually predictable from geometry rather than being a mysterious property of the lifter.

q: A plank gets harder the longer it is held. Why is that different from the other exercises here?
o: Nothing moves, so fatigue builds rather than a moment arm changing
The moment arm increases steadily as the hips drop lower towards the floor
The abdominal muscles shorten progressively as the hold goes on
The load increases with time, since gravity pulls harder as you tire
e: Isometric holds have one position and one demand. What changes is the muscle's capacity to keep meeting it. That is why a plank is progressed by lever length or added load rather than by finding a harder point in the range.

q: Stationary bike: how should the saddle's fore and aft position be set?
o: So the front knee sits over the pedal spindle with the crank level
As far forward as it will go, so the knee sits well ahead of the toes
So the knee sits behind the heel at the bottom of the stroke
Anywhere, since only the saddle height affects the knee
e: Fore and aft position sets where the force is applied relative to the knee. Too far back overextends the reach and loads the back of the knee; too far forward pushes the knee past the foot. Knee over spindle is the working reference.

q: Stationary bike: what does a saddle set too low cause?
o: Too much knee bend through the stroke and load on the front of the knee
Rocking hips and strain behind the knee as the rider reaches down for the pedals
Strain behind the knee from overstretching it
Difficulty keeping the feet on the pedals at speed
e: Never letting the knee open keeps it in deep flexion under load, which is the classic setup cause of anterior knee pain on a bike. It is the opposite failure to a saddle set too high.

q: Rowing machine: what does the damper setting actually change?
o: How much air reaches the flywheel, which changes the feel, not the workload
The total resistance, which works exactly like moving the pin in a weight stack
The stroke rate the machine allows before it limits the flywheel
The distance recorded per stroke, whatever the power applied
e: The damper controls airflow, so a high setting feels heavy and slow and a low setting feels light and fast. Power output depends on how hard you pull, not on where the lever sits, which is why a high damper is not a harder workout by itself.

q: Rowing machine: what does a high stroke rate with low power output usually indicate?
o: Rushing the recovery and pulling with the arms rather than the legs
Excellent technique and efficiency, with the rower moving smoothly at speed
A damper set too high, so the flywheel is slowing each stroke
A seat set too far back on the rail for the rower's legs
e: Power comes from the legs, which take time to apply. Fast, weak strokes are the signature of someone moving the handle rather than the flywheel. Slowing the rate and driving harder usually raises output immediately.

q: Treadmill: why is a one per cent incline sometimes recommended for running?
o: It roughly matches the air resistance of running the same speed outdoors
It reduces impact on the knees by shortening the stride and softening landing
It stops the belt slipping under the foot at higher speeds
It raises the calorie burn substantially at every speed
e: Indoors there is no air to push through. A 1% incline roughly matches the energy cost of running at the same speed outdoors, at moderate to fast paces.

q: Why are handrail heart rate sensors on cardio machines unreliable?
o: Grip, sweat and movement disturb the contact, and holding on alters the work
They measure blood pressure rather than heart rate, so the number is misread
They only work at low intensities, below the level most sessions reach
They are calibrated for one body size, so most users read high
e: The measurement needs steady skin contact, which a moving, sweating hand does not provide. Beyond that, holding the rails offloads bodyweight, so the reading and the workload are both altered by the act of taking it.

q: Elliptical: what does increasing the stride length change?
o: The range of hip and knee movement, and so the muscular demand per stride
Only the calorie readout, since the machine estimates energy from the stride length
The resistance level, which rises automatically with the stride
The impact on the joints, which rises as the stride gets longer
e: A longer stride means more hip extension and flexion per cycle, which asks more of the hip musculature. It is the equivalent of changing range of motion on any other exercise, and it is routinely left on the default.

q: Stair climber: what does leaning on the handrails do?
o: Transfers bodyweight into the arms, cutting the hip extension work
Improves posture and safety, with no real cost to the work being done
Increases the cardiovascular demand by adding the arms
Changes the muscles worked to the upper body and shoulders
e: The point of the machine is repeatedly lifting bodyweight with the hips. Taking weight through the arms removes exactly that. It is the same problem as holding a treadmill's rails, and it is more common because the machine is harder.

q: Glute bridge against barbell hip thrust: what is the real difference?
o: Range of motion, since the shoulders are raised on a bench in a thrust
The muscles worked, since the thrust brings in the quadriceps as well
The bridge loads the hamstrings, and the thrust loads the glutes
There is no meaningful difference, beyond how the bar is balanced
e: Elevating the shoulders lets the hip start in more flexion, so the range is longer and the glutes work through more of it. Same pattern, same peak position, more range and usually more load.

q: Stiff-legged deadlift against Romanian deadlift: what distinguishes them?
o: Stiff-legged keeps the knees nearly straight; the RDL keeps them soft
They are the same exercise, with two names for the same movement
The RDL involves no hip movement, since the knees do the bending
The stiff-legged version loads the quadriceps, since the knees are locked
e: Both are hinges. The differences are knee angle and starting point, which change how much hamstring length is demanded and how much of the lift happens near the floor. The names are often used loosely, which is worth knowing when reading a programme.

q: Cable crossover against a pec deck: what is the substantive difference?
o: The crossover frees the path and elbow angle; the pec deck fixes both
The crossover trains a different muscle, since the hands cross the midline
The pec deck allows more range, since the pads travel further back
The crossover removes the anterior deltoid by pulling from above
e: Both produce horizontal adduction. A cable lets the hands cross the midline and the elbow bend as it likes, which adds range and stabiliser demand. The machine trades that away for a fixed, easily loaded path.
